column1: # CALL-GRAPH STRUCTURAL DIFFERENTIAL — CLOSED INVENTORY.
# WHY THIS EXISTS. GI-11's acceptance was an `observable`: a named Rust test that exists,
# is not ignored, and passes. Measured, an empty `#[test] fn …() {}` produces exactly
# `1 passed`, so the entire structural contract was satisfied by a body of `{}`. That was
# the sixth rung of a ladder this session has climbed repeatedly, and the boundary is:
#     NO CHECK INSIDE THE ARTIFACT CAN ESTABLISH THAT A FUTURE REPLACEMENT IS GENUINE.
# WHY THE FIRST VERSION OF THIS FILE WAS THE SEVENTH RUNG. It asked the provider for a
# STRING and compared it to a fixed one. Measured: a source-keyed stub returning the five
# expected strings scored 5/5. A corpus of expected outputs defeats a provider that
# computes nothing only if the provider cannot know which output is wanted — and a lookup
# table always can.
# WHAT CLOSES IT: FAULT INJECTION, which is already in GI-11's own pinned text and which an
# earlier round wrongly printed as "discharged by human review". Every row carries a
# `mutation` that removes the fact the row is about. The provider is asked twice, and both
# must hold:
#     answer(source)  == expect             the graph is right about the program
#     answer(mutated) == expect-mutated     it is right about a program it has NOT seen
# The second condition was first written as `!= answer(source)` — merely "the answer
# changed" — and a hardcoded table plus a constant fallback scored full marks against it,
# because a constant IS a change. Pinning the OUTCOME closes that: a lookup table has no
# entry for the mutated program, and silence is not an answer either.
# WHAT THIS FILE PINS: scoped call-site identities · declared entry roots · an
# order-independent fixed point · per-edge completion (both ways) · indirect targets
# resolved-or-declared, the last of them PER CALL SITE. Five clauses over eight rows; the
# ROW SET is pinned by EXPECTED_CALLGRAPH_IDS and checked every run, while the clause count
# in this sentence is prose a reviewer checks — an earlier version of this line claimed the
# self-test counted it, and no such case exists.
# PROVENANCE IS NOT A PROPERTY, AND IT IS NOT A PER-ANSWER TAG EITHER. Two narrowings, both
# forced by review. It began as a row of its own, asked as `provider(unit, "provenance")`,
# which proved only that the provider could hash its input and tied that digest to nothing.
# It then became a tag on each per-property answer — and that was refuted too: handing a
# value-only provider a correct digest is free (the self-test's `_bound` does exactly
# that), so the digest never caught a stale VALUE, and querying properties one at a time
# let `edges`, `completion` and `indirect` come from INCONSISTENT snapshots wearing the
# same digest.
# The provider now returns ONE SNAPSHOT PER UNIT — `(provenance, {property: value})` — and
# the runner asks ONCE per unit, caches it, and projects every property from that object.
# What that establishes, exactly: every property the gate reads for a unit comes from one
# object the provider labelled with the digest of the bytes it was handed, so the answers
# cannot be assembled from different snapshots and cannot wear another unit's identity. It
# establishes NOTHING about derivation — a provider that hashes its input while returning a
# remembered graph passes, on purpose, and that is the residue this gate prints rather than
# a hole it hides.
# THE INDIRECT CONTRACT, SETTLED. GI-11's text carries two clauses that read as one:
# "indirect targets resolved or the edge declared unresolved" and "unresolved target =
# HARNESS FAILURE distinct from omission". They name TWO situations, and this is the
# contract the pin now states and this corpus enforces:
#     Every indirect call site is answered either as a RESOLUTION NAMING ONE OR MORE
#     TARGETS or as UNRESOLVED — both discharge the obligation, and omitting the call site
#     silently is a graph FAILURE — while an answer that claims resolution and names NO
#     target is a HARNESS FAILURE distinct from omission, because the gate cannot tell a
#     resolution from a declination and refuses to score the row rather than read it as
#     either.
# So `unresolved` PASSES (an edge whose target cannot be determined is a fact about the
# program, honestly reported), a wrong or absent answer FAILS the row, and `resolved:` with
# an empty target list raises a harness error instead of being scored either way.
# AND THE ANSWER IS KEYED BY SITE, because the sentence above says "every indirect call
# site" and a scalar answer cannot address one: `resolved:a,b` reads equally as two targets
# for one site or one target for each of two sites. `indirect-multi-site` is the program
# that tells them apart, and its mutation removes ONE of two calls.
# WHICH EDGES ARE IN SCOPE. The queries below range over the projection whose CALLEES ARE
# DEFINED IN THE SUBMITTED UNIT. Builtin callees (`panic`, `file_write`, …) are outside it:
# `completion-diverges` expects `main>stop=no` and NOT `stop>panic=no`. This was undefined
# before, and it is the difference between a corpus a real implementation can pass and one
# only an exact-source oracle can — a genuine graph that models builtins answers these
# queries by projecting them out, which is mechanical; guessing which convention the corpus
# meant is not.
# WHAT REMAINS, AND IT IS ONE THING, NOT TWO. Measured this round: an adversary who reads
# this corpus and tabulates the correct answer for every program AND every mutation scores
# 8/8. Run-time metamorphic renaming takes that exact-source table to 0/8 — but an
# adversary that normalises identifiers, looks up, and re-applies the suffix is back to
# 8/8, and it passes the provenance obligation too by hashing whatever it was handed. A
# FINITE, PUBLIC CORPUS CANNOT DEFEAT A READER. What these rows establish is that SPECIFIC
# wrong-answer and exact-table strategies fail — not that a wrong implementation in general
# fails, and not that a real one exists. Implementation authenticity and generalisation
# beyond these eight programs are review obligations at the point GI-11 lands, and the gate
# says exactly that in its output rather than implying the corpus closed it.
# COLUMNS (TAB-separated, all EIGHT mandatory):
#   id  property  source  expect  mutation  expect-mutated  why  source-of-truth
# property: edges | roots | completion | indirect | identical-to
# source:   a whole compilation unit, `\n` for newline. DECODED before the provider sees
#           it — an earlier version passed the TSV encoding through, so a real parser would
#           have received backslash-n.
# answer:   the provider returns ONE SNAPSHOT PER UNIT — `(provenance, {property: value})`
#           — and the gate PROJECTS the properties below from it. `provenance` is the
#           sha256 of the DECODED unit it was handed, computed independently by the runner.
#           A bare value, a stale digest, a snapshot that is not a property map, or a
#           snapshot with no entry for the property fails the row. The runner asks ONCE per
#           unit and caches, so every property of a unit demonstrably comes from one
#           object; see the module docstring of scripts/thesis_exit.py for the one sentence
#           on what that does and does not establish (it does not establish derivation).
# expect:   the value the graph must return.
#   edges         caller>callee, comma-separated, sorted. Scoped where a bare name is
#                 ambiguous: `Buf::len`, not `len`. Callees not defined in the unit are out
#                 of scope. `(none)` when the projection is empty.
#   roots         comma-separated, sorted.
#   completion    caller>callee=yes|no, sorted. `yes` = this edge's callee always returns;
#                 `no` = it may diverge. A fact about the CALLEE, not about whether the
#                 call site is reached — an earlier version conflated the two and marked an
#                 edge into a plainly-returning function `no`.
#   indirect      SITE-KEYED, comma-separated, sorted: `<site>=unresolved` or
#                 `<site>=resolved:<t1>;<t2>`, or `(none)` when the unit has no indirect
#                 call site. A site is `<caller>><callee-expression>`, with `#<n>` in source
#                 order when one caller invokes the same expression more than once.
#                 A SCALAR ANSWER COULD NOT CARRY THIS CONTRACT: `resolved:a,b` cannot
#                 distinguish two targets for ONE site from one target for EACH of two
#                 sites, so "every indirect call site" was enforceable only where there was
#                 exactly one. Where the row writes alternatives separated by `|`, ANY is
#                 accepted: the contract permits resolving or declaring per site, so a
#                 better provider that resolves must not fail a row written for one that
#                 declares. A site that claims `resolved:` and names nothing is a HARNESS
#                 FAILURE, not a score; a dropped site, a duplicate site key and an
#                 unparseable entry are wrong ANSWERS and die in the score.
#   identical-to  the id of another row. The two programs' EDGE SETS are compared to each
#                 other — an earlier version accepted the literal id string, proving nothing.
# mutation: `find=>replace`, applied to the DECODED source. Removing the fact the row is
#           about must change the provider's answer.
# expect-mutated: the answer the MUTATED program must produce. `(none)` means the property
#           is empty for it. REQUIRING A SPECIFIC OUTCOME, not merely a different one, is
#           what closes the last gap: measured, a hardcoded table plus a constant fallback
#           scored full marks against "the answer must change", because a constant IS a
#           change.
#           It cannot produce the right answer for a program it has never seen.
# id
scoped-identity
column7: two functions named `len` in different impls. A bare-name graph collapses them and reports an edge into Log::len that does not exist — the defect measured in src/effects/mod.rs:98. Removing the call must remove the edge

column1: order-independent
column3: fn main() { helper(); }\nfn helper() -> i64 { return 1; }
column5: fn main() { helper(); }=>fn extra() -> i64 { return 2; }\nfn main() { helper(); extra(); }
column7: the same program with its definitions reordered must yield the SAME EDGE SET as `entry-roots`. A single forward pass over source order does not. Removing the call must break the equality

column1: completion-diverges
column7: the callee diverges, so the edge may not complete. Making it return must flip the fact. `panic` is a builtin, so `stop>panic` is outside the projection this corpus queries — see WHICH EDGES ARE IN SCOPE

column1: completion-returns
column3: fn ok() -> i64 { return 1; }\nfn main() { ok(); }
column7: the POSITIVE control the first version lacked: a callee that always returns. Making it diverge must flip the fact

column1: indirect-declared
column3: fn target() -> i64 { return 1; }\nfn run(f: fn() -> i64) -> i64 { return f(); }\nfn main() { run(target); }
column7: the call `f()` has no statically visible target here. The contract permits resolving it OR declaring it unresolved; omitting it silently is the failure this row exists to catch, and `resolved:` naming nothing is a harness failure rather than either. Removing the indirect call must change the answer

column1: indirect-multi-site
column7: TWO indirect sites in ONE caller — the case a scalar answer could not express, and the corpus had none. Each site is answered independently, so all four resolved/unresolved combinations are permitted; removing one of the two calls must drop exactly one entry, which is the fault injection a site-blind answer passes by accident

column1: provenance-binding
column3: fn extra() -> i64 { return 2; }\nfn main() { extra(); }
column7: the named instance of an obligation every row now carries: the unit's whole snapshot arrives as `(provenance, {property: value})` and the provenance must be the digest of the unit submitted, so a graph remembered from another unit cannot wear this one's identity. The mutation changes the unit, so a remembered digest fails too. This does not prove the graph was DERIVED from the unit — only that one labelled object is where all of its answers came from
